name: Tennessee
summary_text:
Trans visitors to Tennessee stand under the United States federal framework as well as state law. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary; the State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed these restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. Passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until expiry, while trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. TSA screening can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments have issued advisories about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules. 
 Tennessee's Adult Entertainment Act of 2023 (SB 3/HB 9) criminalises "adult cabaret entertainment", a definition that expressly includes "male or female impersonators", performed on public property or anywhere a child could see it. A first offence is a Class A misdemeanour carrying up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine; a second violation is a Class E felony carrying 1 to 6 years and fines to $3,000. A trans visitor who performs, or who is perceived as performing, within that definition faces repeat-offence felony exposure after a single prior conviction. 
 The Act survived federal challenge on procedural grounds, and in 2026 the Supreme Court refused to hear challenges to it, leaving the appeals-court ruling upholding the 2023 statute in place. A separate suit over the law remains ongoing. 
 Violence risk is documented at a level well above the national picture. A July 2026 national analysis using TGEU and Williams Institute data records Tennessee's killing rate of trans women at 7.8 per 100,000 per year, based on 10 recorded deaths between 2008 and 2025 and treated as an undercount floor rather than a total. The same analysis places Tennessee in the "Worst Laws Passed" tier of states. 
 Custody is hazardous. In April 2024 the Tennessee State Legislature passed a bill banning gender-affirming care for Tennessee inmates. Under the 2026 Riley Gaines Women's Safety and Protection Act, transgender inmates are to be placed in prisons according to sex assigned at birth, and the same Act bans trans women from women's shelters, removing an access point for a visitor who has no other accommodation.

name: Texas
summary_text: Texas sits under the United States federal framework, which governs the documents a trans visitor presents at the border and in federal settings. Executive Order 14168 of 20 January 2025 defines sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity and prohibits self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department no longer processes the X marker or any marker that does not match sex assigned at birth; new passports are issued only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already carrying an X remain valid until expiry. The Supreme Court allowed those passport restrictions to take effect in November 2025, and the ACLU is suing the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs over confiscated or blocked applications.  Two federal exposures compound the document risk. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement barring trans athletes from entering the country to compete in women's sports, with visa applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex treated as grounds for a permanent fraud-based ban and flagged with an internal marking. TSA checkpoint procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs that are invasive of privacy, and several foreign governments, including at least eight European states, adjusted travel guidance for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the United States during 2025.  Within Texas, the controlling state law is the Women's Privacy Act, signed by Governor Greg Abbott on 22 September 2025 and effective 4 December 2025. It requires restrooms and facilities to be designated by the sex recorded on a birth certificate and applies to public schools, universities, prisons and Texas government buildings. Operators of covered facilities face fines of $25,000 for a first violation and $125,000 for subsequent violations.  Enforcement has begun and has proved uneven. On 6 December 2025, two days after the statute took effect, Texas Department of Public Safety troopers checked identification at women's restrooms outside the state Capitol; trans women holding female ID markers were admitted. Opponents warned that unclear state guidelines produce inconsistent and invasive enforcement, the Austin City Council moved to circumvent the law's intent, and protests followed at the Capitol.  The attorney general, Ken Paxton, has also turned the statute against a school district. In April 2026 his office filed a second complaint escalating a state investigation into Austin ISD over its bathroom policy, issuing a renewed records demand after a tip-line complaint. It is the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry directed at a school district.  A July 2026 anti-trans legal risk assessment, graded law by law across care bans, bathroom bans and enforcement posture using a five-year legislation-tracking methodology, places Texas in the top 'Do Not Travel' tier for adult trans travellers alongside Florida, Idaho and Kansas. Texas is one of four states carrying that tier.  Violence against trans women in Texas is documented at the highest absolute level of any state. A July 2026 national analysis drawing on TGEU and Williams Institute data records 44 killings of trans women in Texas between 2008 and 2025, roughly 7.6 per 100,000 per year, a figure the analysis treats as an undercount floor rather than a ceiling.  Correctional settings carry a documented record of harm. The most recent Texas statute on gender placements reaches prisons only as to restroom use; it does not govern cell or facility assignment or trans-prisoner housing placement. In Gibson v. Collier, Vanessa Lynn Gibson, a transgender woman held by the Texas Department of Criminal Justice and diagnosed with gender dysphoria, was denied gender-confirmation surgery because the department's treatment policy excluded that procedure. A federal district court rejected the state's immunity defences but ruled against her on the Eighth Amendment claim, and the Fifth Circuit affirmed dismissal, holding that refusing the surgery was a permissible medical choice; Judge Barksdale dissented on summary-judgement procedure.
